results.question: How does a UE that is not operating as an IAB-node initiate access to the 5GS?
results.reference: It first performs access control checks to determine if the access is allowed, as required for the specific access attempt events listed.
results.model_answer:
A UE that is not operating as an IAB-node initiates access to the 5G System (5GS) by following a standardized NAS-driven procedure defined in **3GPP TS 24.501**, involving **access control checks**, **categorization of the access attempt**, and conditional initiation of **NAS signaling procedures** based on network permission. The process is triggered when the UE needs to transition from an idle or inactive state to a connected state over 3GPP access, due to specific events requiring communication with the network. Below is the step-by-step analysis of how such a UE initiates access: --- ### **1. Triggering Events for Access Attempt** According to the specification, the UE performs access control checks upon occurrence of one of the following events: #### **a) From 5GMM-IDLE or 5GMM-IDLE with suspend indication:** - An event occurs that requires transitioning to **5GMM-CONNECTED** mode. #### **b) From 5GMM-CONNECTED or 5GMM-CONNECTED with RRC INACTIVE indication:** The following mobile-originated (MO) requests trigger an access attempt: 1. MO-IMS registration-related signaling 2. MO-MMTEL voice/video call 3. MO-SMSoIP attempt 4. UL NAS TRANSPORT for PDU session establishment/modification 5. Re-establishment of user-plane resources 6. Uplink data pending for suspended PDU session 7. MO location request 8. MO signaling transaction toward PCF via UL NAS TRANSPORT with UE policy container > **Note:** Procedures initiated directly by NAS (e.g., registration after handover) are **not subject to access control** (see NOTE2). --- ### **2. Access Control Check Initiation** When any of the above events occur, the **NAS layer** determines whether access is allowed through **Access Barring Control**. - The NAS maps the nature of the request to: - One **access category** - One or more **access identities** These are determined using: - Standardized access identities and categories (defined in **TS 22.261**) - Operator-defined access categories (if available) The mapping rules depend on: - Whether the UE is operating in **SNPN access mode** or not. - If **not in SNPN mode**: use **subclause 4.5.2**, tables **4.5.2.1** (identities), **4.5.2.2** (categories) - If **in SNPN mode**: use **subclause 4.5.2A**, tables **4.5.2A.1** and **4.5.2A.2** > This categorization enables lower layers (e.g., RRC/PHY) to perform **access barring checks** based on configured barring parameters per access category. --- ### **3. Providing Access Parameters to Lower Layers** Once categorized: - The NAS provides the **applicable access identities** and **access category** to the **lower layers**. - Optionally, it may also provide the **RRC establishment cause** (as defined in subclause 4.5.6). - Alternatively, this can be provided later if implementation chooses (per NOTE2). > This allows the lower layers to evaluate whether the access attempt is currently barred (e.g., due to congestion or overload). --- ### **4. Handling of Uplink Data in Initial NAS Message** If the UE has **uplink user data pending** for one or more PDU sessions at the time of building the initial NAS message (e.g., REGISTRATION REQUEST or SERVICE REQUEST): - It **shall indicate** those PDU sessions in the **Uplink data status IE**. - For regular service: included in **SERVICE REQUEST** (clause 5.6.1.2.1) - For CP-CIoT optimized UEs: included in **CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST** (clause 5.6.1.2.2) > This indication is done **regardless of the access category being barred or not**, ensuring the network is aware of buffered data once access is granted. --- ### **5. Decision Based on Access Barring Result** After providing access parameters, the NAS waits for feedback from lower layers: #### ✅ **If access is allowed:** - NAS **initiates transmission** of the **initial NAS message** (e.g., REGISTRATION REQUEST, SERVICE REQUEST, etc.). #### ❌ **If access is barred:** - NAS **does not initiate** the NAS procedure. - Behavior depends on the type of access attempt: | Trigger Event | UE Action | |--------------|----------| | **MO-MMTEL Voice/Video Call** |
  • If single-registration + "voice centric" + E-UTRA capable → attempt fallback to EPC via E-UTRA
  • If dual-registration → proceed in S1 mode
  • Otherwise → notify upper layers; retry when barring is alleviated
| | **MO-SMSoIP / IMS Registration Signaling** |
  • Attempt fallback to EPC (single-reg)
  • Proceed in S1 mode (dual-reg)
  • Else → notify upper layers; retry later
| | **Emergency Access** | Notify upper layers; await relief of barring before retrying | > Barring timers run per access category in lower layers. Upon expiry, NAS is informed and may reattempt. --- ### **Summary: Step-by-Step Flow** 1. **Event occurs** (e.g., MO call, uplink data, location request). 2. **NAS detects event** via upper-layer indication or internal logic. 3. **NAS determines access category and identities** based on service type, UE profile, and SNPN status. 4. **NAS provides access category, identities, and optionally RRC cause** to lower layers. 5. **Lower layers perform access barring check**. 6. **If allowed**: - NAS sends initial NAS message (e.g., SERVICE REQUEST). - Includes **Uplink Data Status IE** if data is pending. 7. **If barred**: - NAS defers procedure. - Applies fallback logic (e.g., EPC redirection) where applicable. - Waits for debarment signal before retrying. --- ### **Key Notes** - **IAB-nodes skip access control checks**, but standard UEs do not. - **Access barring is enforced per access category**, managed via timers in lower layers. - **CAG and SNPN-specific behaviors modify access rules**, but only if applicable. - **Emergency services** are never blocked permanently — UE retries upon debarment. --- ### ✅ Final Answer: A UE that is not operating as an IAB-node initiates access to the 5GS by: 1. Detecting an event requiring network connectivity (e.g., MO call, uplink data, registration update). 2. Performing **access control checks** by determining the appropriate **access category** and **access identities** according to its operational mode (SNPN or non-SNPN). 3. Providing these parameters (and optionally the RRC establishment cause) to **lower layers** for **access barring evaluation**. 4. If access is **allowed**, initiating the relevant **NAS signaling procedure** (e.g., Service Request, Registration Request), including **Uplink Data Status** if data is pending. 5. If access is **barred**, deferring the procedure and potentially triggering **fallback mechanisms** (e.g., EPC access) depending on the service type, or waiting for **debarment notification** before retrying. This ensures controlled, prioritized, and policy-compliant access to the 5G core network.

results.question: Why does a UE operating as an IAB-node still determine an access category and access identities for an access attempt?
results.reference: To derive an RRC establishment cause, which the NAS provides to lower layers, even though the IAB-node skips the access control checks.
results.model_answer:
A UE operating as an IAB-node still determines an access category and one or more access identities for an access attempt **to derive the RRC establishment cause**, even though it skips the actual access control (i.e., access barring) checks.

### Reasoning Based on 3GPP TS 24.501:

According to the provided context:

> *"Although the UE operating as an IAB-node skips the access control checks, the UE operating as an IAB-node determines an access category and one or more access identities for each access attempt in order to derive an RRC establishment cause."*

This means that while **access barring** (which is performed by lower layers based on access categories and identities) is skipped for IAB-nodes, the **categorization of the access attempt** into an access category and access identities remains necessary for a different purpose: **RRC layer signaling**.

Specifically:
- The NAS in the IAB-node is responsible for providing the **RRC establishment cause** to the lower layers.
- The mapping from an access attempt to an **RRC establishment cause** depends on the determined **access category and access identities**, as defined in **subclause 4.5.6** of TS 24.501.
- Therefore, even without performing access control, the NAS must still classify the access so that the correct **RRC connection establishment reason** (e.g., mo-Signalling, mo-Data, emergency, etc.) can be derived and communicated to the RRC layer.

### Key Point:
The determination of access category and identities is **not solely for access control**, but also serves as input for **procedure selection and inter-layer coordination**, particularly between NAS and RRC. For IAB-nodes, this information is used internally to ensure proper RRC behavior during connection setup, despite bypassing access barring.

---

### Conclusion:
> A UE operating as an IAB-node determines access categories and access identities **to enable derivation of the RRC establishment cause**, which is required for proper RRC procedure initiation, even though access control (barring) checks are skipped.

results.question: How does the UE enable access barring checks for access attempts identified by lower layers when in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication?
results.reference: The UE provides the applicable access identities to lower layers, though the timing and method of this provision are implementation specific.
results.model_answer:
The UE enables access barring checks for access attempts identified by lower layers when in **5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication** by providing the **applicable access identities and access category** to the lower layers. This allows the lower layers to perform access barring checks based on these parameters.

### Key Mechanism:

1. **Access Identity and Category Determination (NAS Layer):**  
   When an event occurs that triggers an access attempt while the UE is in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication, the NAS layer determines:
   - One or more **access identities**, and
   - One **access category**

   This determination is based on:
   - The reason for access,
   - The type of service requested,
   - UE profile and configuration,
   - Standardized definitions from **3GPP TS 22.261**, including:
     - Standardized access identities,
     - Standardized access categories,
     - Operator-defined access categories (if available).

   The rules for mapping are specified in:
   - **Subclause 4.5.2 and Table 4.5.2.1/4.5.2.2** (for non-SNPN access mode), or
   - **Subclause 4.5.2A and Table 4.5.2A.1/4.5.2A.2** (for SNPN access mode).

2. **Provision to Lower Layers:**  
   The NAS provides the determined **access identities** and **access category** to the lower layers (AS/RRC). This is explicitly stated in the specification:

   > *"In order to enable access barring checks for access attempts identified by lower layers in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication, the UE provides the applicable access identities to lower layers."*

   Although the exact timing and method are implementation-specific (see NOTE6), the provision of this information is mandatory for enabling access control at the AS level.

3. **Lower Layer Performs Access Barring Check:**  
   Once the lower layers receive the access identity and category:
   - They perform **access barring checks** using configured barring parameters (e.g., barring factors, timers per access category).
   - If access is allowed, the RRC connection can be resumed.
   - If access is barred, the attempt is blocked unless exceptions apply (e.g., emergency services, ongoing IMS calls, etc.).

4. **RRC Establishment Cause Derivation:**  
   The NAS also determines the **RRC establishment cause** based on the access category and identities (per **subclause 4.5.6**) and may provide it to lower layers along with the access parameters.

---

### Summary:

To enable access barring checks in **5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication**, the UE:

✅ Determines the appropriate **access identities** and **access category** based on the triggering event and service type.  
✅ Provides these parameters to the **lower layers**.  
✅ Enables the **AS layer** to perform access barring evaluation before resuming the RRC connection.  

This mechanism ensures that even though the UE is in a connected NAS state (with suspended RRC), network-controlled access restrictions are still enforced on new uplink data or signalling triggers.

results.question: What determines which subclause and table a UE uses to find the applicable access category from the standardized and operator-defined sets?
results.reference: It depends on whether the UE is operating in SNPN access mode. If not, it uses subclause 4.5.2 and table 4.5.2.2; if it is, it uses subclause 4.5.2A and table 4.5.2A.2.
results.model_answer:
The determination of which subclause and table a UE uses to find the applicable access category from the standardized and operator-defined sets depends on the **access mode of the UE**, specifically whether the UE is operating in **SNPN (Stand-Alone Non-Public Network) access mode** or not.

This selection is governed by the following rule, derived from the provided context in TS 24.501:

> For the purpose of determining the applicable access category from the set of standardized access categories and operator-defined access categories:
> - The UE shall follow the requirements in **subclause 4.5.2 and use table 4.5.2.2**, if the UE is **not operating in SNPN access mode**.
> - The UE shall follow the requirements in **subclause 4.5.2A and use table 4.5.2A.2**, if the UE is **operating in SNPN access mode**.

### Key Conditions:
- **If UE is in SNPN access mode** → Use **subclause 4.5.2A** and **table 4.5.2A.2**  
- **Otherwise (i.e., public network access via PLMN)** → Use **subclause 4.5.2** and **table 4.5.2.2**

### Additional Notes:
- The same logic applies for determining access identities: subclause 4.5.2 and table 4.5.2.1 for non-SNPN; subclause 4.5.2A and table 4.5.2A.1 for SNPN.
- The UE determines its current access mode based on whether it is registered to or selecting an SNPN versus a public PLMN.
- Operator-defined access categories are evaluated only when valid definitions are stored for the selected or registered PLMN or SNPN.
- If multiple operator-defined access category definitions match, the one with the **lowest precedence value** is selected.
- If no applicable access identity is found among 1, 2, 3, 11–15 (or their SNPN equivalents), then **access identity 0** is used by default.

Thus, the **UE’s access mode (SNPN vs. non-SNPN)** is the primary factor that determines which subclause and table are used for access category determination.

results.question: Under what conditions is the SMF permitted to include the IP header compression configuration IE?
results.reference: The SMF may include it only when all three conditions are met: the network accepts an IP PDU session type, control plane CIoT 5GS optimization is selected, and the UE provided the same IE in its PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message.
results.model_answer:
The SMF is permitted to include the **IP header compression configuration IE** under the following conditions:

1. **General Re-negotiation Case (Network-Requested PDU Session Modification):**  
   The SMF may include the IP header compression configuration IE in a **PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND** message if:
   - Control plane CIoT 5GS optimization is enabled for the PDU session;
   - The UE previously included the IP header compression configuration IE in either the **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST** or **PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST** message;
   - The SMF supports both control plane CIoT 5GS optimization and IP header compression for control plane CIoT 5GS optimization.

   > This allows the SMF to re-negotiate the IP header compression configuration associated with the PDU session during a network-initiated modification.

2. **Conditional Inclusion Based on UE Indication (Implicit from Procedure Logic):**  
   Additionally, while not explicitly stated as a "may" condition, the specification implies that inclusion is only meaningful when:
   - The PDU session type is one of: **"IPv4"**, **"IPv6"**, or **"IPv4v6"** — since IP header compression applies only to IP-based PDU sessions.
   - Both the UE and the network have indicated support for **control plane CIoT 5GS optimization** and specifically **IP header compression for control plane CIoT 5GS optimization** during registration (via 5GMM capability and 5GS network feature support IEs).

3. **Explicit Conditional Allowance (from provided context):**  
   The SMF may include the IP header compression configuration IE if:
   - The network accepts an **IP PDU session type** ("IPv4", "IPv6", or "IPv4v6");
   - **Control plane CIoT 5GS optimization is selected**;
   - The **UE provided the IP header compression configuration IE** in the **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST** message.

   > Note: This condition aligns with initial establishment; however, the SMF may also include it later during modification if the UE re-requests it in a modification request.

---

### ✅ Summary: Conditions Under Which the SMF May Include the IP Header Compression Configuration IE

The SMF is **permitted (may)** include the IP header compression configuration IE in a NAS message (typically *PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND*) **if all of the following are true**:

- The PDU session type is **IPv4**, **IPv6**, or **IPv4v6**;
- **Control plane CIoT 5GS optimization is selected/enabled** for the session;
- The **UE has indicated support** for IP header compression via inclusion of the IE in a prior request (establishment or modification);
- The **SMF supports IP header compression** for control plane CIoT 5GS optimization;
- The procedure involves re-negotiation (e.g., during network-requested modification triggered after UE indication or due to internal network decision).

> ⚠️ **Note:** The SMF does **not** include this IE unilaterally — its inclusion is conditioned on mutual support and prior UE signaling indicating interest in IP header compression negotiation.

Thus, the SMF’s permission to include the IE is **conditional and bidirectional**, requiring alignment in capabilities, session type, optimization mode, and prior UE signaling.

results.question: How does the selection of control plane CIoT 5GS optimization relate to the IP header compression configuration?
results.reference: Control plane CIoT 5GS optimization must be selected as one of the three necessary conditions for the SMF to include the IP header compression configuration IE.
results.model_answer:
The selection of **control plane CIoT 5GS optimization** is a **prerequisite condition** for the negotiation and use of **IP header compression configuration** in 5G NAS procedures, but IP header compression itself is an **optional enhancement** enabled only when additional specific support indications are present from both the UE and the network.

### Analytical Breakdown:

#### 1. **Control Plane CIoT 5GS Optimization Enables Control Plane Data Transport**
- The control plane CIoT 5GS optimization allows small data transfers (including IP, Ethernet, Unstructured, and SMS) over the NAS signaling path via the AMF, without establishing user-plane resources.
- This optimization is particularly intended for IoT devices with limited capabilities (e.g., NB-IoT UEs in NB-N1 mode), where minimizing signaling and resource usage is critical.

#### 2. **IP Header Compression Is Conditional on Control Plane CIoT 5GS Optimization Support**
- According to the specification, **both the UE and the network must indicate support for:**
  - "Control Plane CIoT 5GS optimization supported", **and**
  - "IP header compression for control plane CIoT 5GS optimization supported"
- These indications occur during registration:
  - UE indicates support in the **5GMM capability IE** of the **REGISTRATION REQUEST**.
  - Network confirms support in the **5GS network feature support IE** of the **REGISTRATION ACCEPT**.
- Only if **both sides support these features**, can IP header compression be negotiated for a PDU session.

#### 3. **PDU Session Type Must Be Compatible**
- The PDU session type must be **IPv4**, **IPv6**, or **IPv4v6** for IP header compression to apply.
- This ensures that the data being transported actually contains IP headers suitable for compression.

#### 4. **Negotiation Occurs During PDU Session Procedures**
- Once the preconditions are met, the actual **IP header compression configuration** is negotiated between the UE and SMF using the **IP header compression configuration IE**.
- This negotiation happens during:
  - **PDU Session Establishment** (if included by UE and accepted by SMF),
  - **PDU Session Modification** (for re-negotiation or initial setup after inter-system change).

#### 5. **Mandatory Negotiation After Inter-System Change (S1 → N1)**
- If a UE moves from E-UTRAN (S1 mode) to NR (N1 mode) in single-registration mode with N26 interface support, and:
  - The PDU session is IPv4/IPv6/IPv4v6,
  - Both UE and network support control plane CIoT optimization and IP header compression,
- Then the UE **shall initiate a PDU session modification procedure** to negotiate IP header compression configuration — even if no other changes are needed.

#### 6. **ROHC Is Used for IP Header Compression**
- The actual compression follows **RFC 5795 (ROHC)**, which reduces overhead of IP/UDP/RTP headers.
- The configuration parameters (profiles, modes, etc.) are exchanged via the **IP header compression configuration IE** during session establishment/modification.

---

### Summary of Relationship:

| Condition | Requirement |
|--------|-------------|
| **Control plane CIoT 5GS optimization selected?** | Yes — required as foundation |
| **Is IP header compression automatically used?** | No — only if explicitly supported and negotiated |
| **What triggers inclusion of IP header compression config?** | Both UE and network must signal support during registration AND PDU session is IP-type |
| **When is it negotiated?** | During PDU session establishment or modification |
| **Special case:** Inter-system change S1→N1? | UE **shall** initiate modification to negotiate compression if conditions are met |

> ✅ **Conclusion**:  
> The **selection of control plane CIoT 5GS optimization is necessary but not sufficient** for IP header compression. It creates the architectural context where such optimizations are meaningful. However, **IP header compression configuration is only negotiated if both UE and network explicitly support it**, and the PDU session type permits it. Thus, control plane CIoT optimization enables the *possibility* of efficient transport, while IP header compression provides an *additional efficiency gain* within that framework.

results.question: Under what conditions may the UE radio capability ID information element be included in a message?
results.reference: The IE may be included when three conditions are simultaneously met: the UE is not operating in NB-N1 mode, both the UE and the network support RACS, and the network needs to assign a network-assigned UE radio capability ID to the UE.
results.model_answer:
The **UE radio capability ID Information Element (IE)** may be included in a NAS message under the following conditions, based on 3GPP TS 24.501 and the provided context:

---

### ✅ **1. In Uplink Messages from the UE (e.g., REGISTRATION REQUEST):**

The UE may include the **UE radio capability ID IE** as a *non-cleartext IE* when:
- The UE supports **RACS (UE Radio Capability Signalling Optimisation)**.
- The UE is **not in NB-N1 mode** (i.e., operates in normal N1 mode).
- The UE has an **applicable UE radio capability ID** for its current radio configuration in the selected network.

#### Specific cases:
a) **Initial Registration**  
   - If the UE performs **initial registration** and has an applicable UE radio capability ID, it shall include it.

b) **Mobility or Periodic Registration Update**  
   - If the UE initiates registration due to mobility (e.g., entering a new tracking area not in the registered list), and has an applicable UE radio capability ID, it shall include it.

c) **Radio Configuration Change**  
   - If the UE's radio capabilities change (e.g., disabling a radio), and it has an applicable UE radio capability ID for the new configuration, it shall initiate a registration update and include the ID.

d) **Revocation of Network-Assigned ID**  
   - If the serving PLMN/SNPN revokes previously assigned IDs, and a new applicable ID exists (manufacturer or network-assigned), the UE includes it during the next registration.

#### Priority Rule:
- If both **network-assigned** and **manufacturer-assigned** UE radio capability IDs are applicable, the UE **shall include the network-assigned UE radio capability ID**.

> ⚠️ Note: The UE must set the **RACS bit to "supported"** in the 5GMM capability IE whenever sending a REGISTRATION REQUEST that includes the UE radio capability ID IE (except for periodic updates).

---

### ✅ **2. In Downlink Messages from the Network (e.g., REGISTRATION ACCEPT, CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND):**

The network may include the **UE radio capability ID IE** when:
- The network supports RACS.
- The UE supports RACS.
- The UE is **not in NB-N1 mode**.
- The network wishes to **assign a new network-assigned UE radio capability ID** to the UE.

#### Valid messages:
- `REGISTRATION ACCEPT`
- `CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND`

> Upon receiving this IE, the UE shall store the ID along with the PLMN/SNPN identity and current radio configuration in non-volatile memory.

---

### ❌ **When the UE Radio Capability ID IE Shall NOT Be Included:**
- The UE is in **NB-N1 mode** → RACS is not applicable.
- The UE does **not support RACS**.
- The network does **not support RACS**.
- The UE has **no applicable UE radio capability ID** (in which case it signals need for update via NG-RAN-RCU bit instead).
- The UE is performing procedures over **non-3GPP access** → RACS is not applicable.

---

### 📝 Summary of Conditions for Inclusion:

| Condition | Required? | Notes |
|--------|----------|-------|
| UE supports RACS | ✅ Yes | Must set RACS bit in 5GMM capability |
| Network supports RACS | ✅ Yes | Otherwise no assignment possible |
| Access is 3GPP (N1 mode) | ✅ Yes | Not supported over non-3GPP or NB-N1 |
| UE is not in NB-N1 mode | ✅ Yes | Explicitly excluded per spec |
| Applicable UE radio capability ID exists | ✅ Yes | Either manufacturer- or network-assigned |
| Message type allows non-cleartext IEs | ✅ Yes | Requires NAS message container if needed |

---

### ✅ Supported Message Types:
The **UE radio capability ID IE** can appear in:
- `REGISTRATION REQUEST` (uplink, non-cleartext)
- `REGISTRATION ACCEPT` (downlink)
- `CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND` (downlink)

---

### 🔁 Additional Behavior:
- If the network sends a **UE radio capability ID deletion indication**, the UE deletes stored network-assigned IDs and may later re-submit a **manufacturer-assigned ID** in a subsequent registration.
- The UE stores up to **16 network-assigned IDs** with associated context.

---

### Conclusion:
> The **UE radio capability ID IE** may be included in a NAS message **if and only if**:  
> - The UE and network both support RACS,  
> - The UE is operating in **normal N1 mode (not NB-N1)**,  
> - The access is **3GPP**,  
> - An applicable UE radio capability ID exists (and network-assigned takes precedence),  
> - And the message direction and type permit it (e.g., REGISTRATION REQUEST/ACCEPT, CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND).

results.question: What capability must both the UE and network possess for the UE radio capability ID IE to be included?
results.reference: Both the UE and the network must support RACS (Radio Capability Signaling optimization).
results.model_answer:
For the **UE radio capability ID IE** to be included in a NAS message, both the **UE and the network must support RACS (UE Radio Capability Signalling Optimisation)**.

### Reasoning:
The inclusion of the **UE radio capability ID IE** is directly tied to the use of the **RACS feature**, which allows the UE to signal a compact identifier (the UE radio capability ID) instead of transmitting the full UE radio capability information over the air.

From the provided context:

> "This IE shall be included if the UE is not in NB-N1 mode, the UE supports RACS and the UE needs to signal a UE radio capability ID to the network"

Additionally, earlier clauses clarify that:
- The UE indicates support for RACS by setting the **RACS bit** in the 5GMM capability IE.
- The network may assign or request deletion of UE radio capability IDs only if it also supports RACS.
- The actual use of the **UE radio capability ID IE** assumes mutual support — otherwise, the full UE radio capabilities would need to be signalled instead.

Moreover, subclause conditions (e.g., during registration procedures) state that the UE includes the UE radio capability ID **only if it has an applicable one and supports RACS**, and the network must also support RACS for such identifiers to be meaningful (e.g., for assignment via `REGISTRATION ACCEPT` or `CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND`).

Also note: RACS is **not applicable** in **NB-N1 mode** or over **non-3GPP access**, so the IE cannot be used in those contexts regardless of support.

---

### Final Answer:
Both the **UE and the network must support RACS**, and the UE must not be in NB-N1 mode.

results.question: What actions must the AUSF take upon successful authentication when it acts as the EAP-AKA' server?
results.reference: The AUSF must generate EMSK, derive KAUSF from EMSK, and derive KSEAF from KAUSF as specified in 3GPP TS 33.501.
results.model_answer:
When the AUSF acts as the EAP-AKA' server and authentication is successful, the following actions must be taken by the AUSF based on 3GPP TS 24.501 and referenced specifications: ### 1. **Generate Cryptographic Keys** Upon successful handling of the `EAP-response/AKA'-challenge` message: - The AUSF **shall generate the EMSK** (Extended Master Session Key) as specified in IETF RFC 5448. - From the EMSK, the AUSF **shall derive the KAUSF** (Key at AUSF) using the key derivation function defined in **3GPP TS 33.501**. - Then, the AUSF **shall derive the KSEAF** (Key at SEAF) from the KAUSF, also per **TS 33.501**. > ✅ *Relevant text: "a) the AUSF acts as the EAP-AKA' server, the AUSF shall generate EMSK, the KAUSF from the EMSK, and the KSEAF from the KAUSF as described in 3GPPTS33.501[24]"* --- ### 2. **Handle AT_RESULT_IND Attribute Logic** The AUSF must evaluate whether to send an `EAP-success` or `EAP-request/AKA'-notification` based on inclusion and presence of the `AT_RESULT_IND` attribute: - If the AUSF **included AT_RESULT_IND** in the `EAP-request/AKA'-challenge` **and** it is **present** in the `EAP-response/AKA'-challenge`, then: - Send an **EAP-request/AKA'-notification** message (success indication). - Else (i.e., either AT_RESULT_IND was not included, or it's missing in the response): - Send an **EAP-Success** message and consider the EAP authentication procedure complete. > ✅ *Relevant logic: “if the AUSF ... included the AT_RESULT_IND attribute [...] and the AT_RESULT_IND attribute is included in the corresponding EAP-response... shall send an EAP-request/AKA'-notification”; otherwise, send EAP-Success.* Note: Even when sending an `EAP-request/AKA'-notification`, the procedure may still conclude with a subsequent `EAP-Success`. However, if conditions for notification are not met, `EAP-Success` follows directly after challenge response. --- ### 3. **Forward Security Material to SEAF** After deriving KSEAF: - The AUSF **shall provide the KSEAF** (and optionally the SUPI, if not already available to the SEAF) to the **SEAF (Security Anchor Function)** as specified in **TS 33.501**. This enables the SEAF to proceed with generating the **KAMF** (Key at AMF), which is essential for NAS security context establishment in the AMF. > ✅ *From NOTE2: “The AUSF provides the KSEAF and optionally the SUPI [...] to the SEAF [...]”* --- ### Summary: Actions Required by AUSF | Step | Action | |------|-------| | 1 | Generate **EMSK** from successful EAP-AKA' exchange | | 2 | Derive **KAUSF** from EMSK per TS 33.501 | | 3 | Derive **KSEAF** from KAUSF per TS 33.501 | | 4 | Evaluate `AT_RESULT_IND`:
– If present in both request and response → send `EAP-request/AKA'-notification`
– Otherwise → send `EAP-Success` | | 5 | Forward **KSEAF** (and SUPI if needed) to the **SEAF** | These steps ensure mutual authentication, secure key hierarchy establishment, and proper progression toward creating a partial native 5G NAS security context in the AMF via SEAF.

results.question: How does the network proceed when the AT_RESULT_IND attribute was included in the challenge request but is missing from the UE's response?
results.reference: The AUSF or AAA server must send an EAP-success message and consider the authentication procedure complete.
results.model_answer:
When the **AT_RESULT_IND attribute** is included in the **EAP-request/AKA'-challenge** message but is **missing from the UE's EAP-response/AKA'-challenge** message, the network (i.e., the AUSF or the AAA server of the CH/DCS) proceeds as follows:

According to the provided context from 3GPP TS 24.501:

> b) if the AUSF or the AAA server of the CH or the DCS  
> 1) included the AT_RESULT_IND attribute in the EAP-request/AKA'-challenge message and the AT_RESULT_IND attribute is not included in the EAP-response/AKA'-challenge message; or  
> 2) did not include the AT_RESULT_IND attribute in the EAP-request/AKA'-challenge message  
> then the AUSF or the AAA server of the CH or the DCS shall send an **EAP-success message** as specified in IETF RFC 5448 [40] and shall consider the procedure complete.

### Therefore:
- The **inclusion** of `AT_RESULT_IND` in the challenge request indicates that the network expects an explicit result indication from the UE.
- However, if the UE **does not include** `AT_RESULT_IND` in its response, this falls under condition **b)1)** above.
- Despite the missing attribute in the response, the specification **does not require the network to reject or fail the authentication**.
- Instead, the network **shall proceed to send an EAP-Success message**, treating the EAP-AKA' authentication as successful, and **consider the procedure complete**.

### Conclusion:
The network **does not treat the absence of AT_RESULT_IND in the UE’s response as a failure**. Even though the UE did not echo back the expected attribute, the network **sends an EAP-Success message and completes the EAP-based authentication procedure**.

This behavior ensures robustness in cases where the UE may not support or properly handle the result indication, while still allowing the network to finalize the authentication when other credentials (e.g., RES) are valid.

results.question: What key generation steps occur when a AAA server acts as the EAP-AKA' server?
results.reference: The AAA server generates MSK as described in TS 33.501, provides MSK and SUPI to AUSF via NSSAAF, then AUSF derives KAUSF from MSK and KSEAF from KAUSF.
results.model_answer:
When a **AAA server of the Credentials Holder (CH) or the Default Credentials Server (DCS)** acts as the **EAP-AKA' server**, the following key generation steps occur, based on 3GPP TS 24.501 and referenced specifications:

---

### 1. **MSK Generation by the AAA Server**
- Upon successful completion of the EAP-AKA' authentication challenge-response exchange:
  - The **AAA server (acting as EAP-AKA' server)** generates the **Master Session Key (MSK)** as defined in **IETF RFC 5448** and **3GPP TS 33.501**.
  - This MSK is derived from the AKA' run using the shared secret stored in the USIM (K), along with network-provided parameters such as AUTN, RAND, etc.

> ✅ *Relevant specification text:*
> > "b) the AAA server of the CH or the DCS acts as the EAP-AKA' server, the AAA server of the CH or the DCS shall generate MSK as described in 3GPPTS33.501[24]"

---

### 2. **Forwarding MSK and SUPI to AUSF via NSSAAF**
- After generating the MSK, the AAA server:
  - Provides the **MSK** and the **SUPI (Subscription Permanent Identifier)** to the **AUSF** via the **NSSAAF (Network Slice-Specific Authentication and Authorization Function)** interface.

> ✅ *From NOTE1 in the context:*
> > "The AAA server of the CH or the DCS provides (via the NSSAAF) the MSK and the SUPI to the AUSF."

---

### 3. **KAUSF Derivation at the AUSF**
- Upon receiving the MSK and SUPI:
  - The **AUSF derives the KAUSF (Key for AUSF)** from the **MSK**, using a key derivation function defined in **3GPP TS 33.501**.
    - Specifically:  
      `KAUSF = KDF(MSK, "5G AUSF key" || SNN)`
      where SNN is the Serving Network Name.

> ✅ *From NOTE1:*
> > "Upon reception of the MSK, the AUSF generates the KAUSF from the MSK [...] as described in 3GPPTS33.501[24]"

---

### 4. **KSEAF Derivation at the AUSF**
- Using the derived **KAUSF**, the AUSF then computes the **KSEAF (Key for SEAF)**:
  - `KSEAF = KDF(KAUSF, "5G SEAF key" || SNN)`

> ✅ *Same note continues:*
> > "...and the KSEAF from the KAUSF as described in 3GPPTS33.501[24]"

---

### 5. **Provisioning KSEAF to SEAF**
- The AUSF sends the **KSEAF** and optionally the **SUPI** (if not already known) to the **SEAF (Security Anchor Function)**.
- The SEAF uses this key material to derive the **KAMF (Key for AMF)** later during the SEAF-AMF interaction.

> ✅ *From NOTE3:*
> > "The AUSF provides the KSEAF and optionally the SUPI [...] to the SEAF [...] Upon reception of the KSEAF and optionally the SUPI, the SEAF generates the KAMF based on the ABBA, the KSEAF and the SUPI..."

---

### Summary of Key Generation Flow (AAA as EAP-AKA' Server):

```
UE (USIM)
   │
   ├── EAP-AKA' Exchange (RAND, AUTN, RES, etc.)
   ▼
AAA Server (EAP-AKA' Server)
   │
   ├── Generates MSK per RFC 5448 / TS 33.501
   │
   └── Sends MSK + SUPI → AUSF via NSSAAF
         │
         ▼
       AUSF
         │
         ├── Derives KAUSF from MSK
         │
         └── Derives KSEAF from KAUSF
               │
               └──→ Sends KSEAF (+ SUPI) → SEAF
```

---

### Important Notes:
- The **EMSK (Extended MSK)** is **not used** when the AAA server acts as EAP-AKA' server — only **MSK** is generated.
- The actual **KAMF** is derived later by the **SEAF**, using:
  - `KAMF = KDF(KSEAF, "5G AMF key" || ABBA || SUPI)`
  - Where **ABBA** is an anti-binding assurance parameter sent during EAP messaging.

---

### Conclusion:
When the **AAA server (CH/DCS)** acts as the **EAP-AKA' server**:
1. It **generates the MSK** after successful authentication.
2. It **forwards the MSK and SUPI to the AUSF**.
3. The **AUSF derives KAUSF from the MSK**, then **KSEAF from KAUSF**.
4. These keys enable secure derivation of **KAMF** in the SEAF for NAS security establishment.

This process ensures that even though the AUSF does not directly perform EAP-AKA', it still participates in deriving the necessary 5G authentication keys through trusted input from the AAA server.

results.question: Under what condition must the AUSF or AAA server send an EAP-request/AKA'-notification message?
results.reference: When both the challenge request and corresponding response include the AT_RESULT_IND attribute.
results.model_answer:
The AUSF or the AAA server of the CH or the DCS **must send an EAP-request/AKA'-notification message** under the following two conditions:

---

### 1. **Upon reception of the EAP-response/AKA'-challenge message, if the EAP-AKA' challenge response handling fails**

As per the specification:
> "Upon reception of the EAP-response/AKA'-challenge message, if procedures for handling an EAP-response/AKA'-challenge message as specified in IETFRFC5448[40] are not successful, the AUSF or the AAA server of the CH or the DCS shall send an EAP-request/AKA'-notification message that implies failure as specified in IETFRFC5448[40]."

This applies when:
- The UE's response (e.g., RES in AT_RES) is invalid.
- Cryptographic verification fails (e.g., MAC check failure).
- Any other EAP-AKA' peer/server processing step fails.

👉 In this case, the network sends an **EAP-request/AKA'-notification** indicating **failure**, before proceeding to either retry authentication or reject it.

---

### 2. **When the AT_RESULT_IND attribute was included in the EAP-request/AKA'-challenge and is also present in the EAP-response/AKA'-challenge**

As per the specification:
> "If the AUSF or the AAA server of the CH or the DCS included the AT_RESULT_IND attribute in the EAP-request/AKA'-challenge message and the AT_RESULT_IND attribute is included in the corresponding EAP-response/AKA'-challenge message, the AUSF or the AAA server of the CH or the DCS shall send an EAP-request/AKA'-notification message as specified in IETFRFC5448[40]."

This is a **conditional success indication**:  
Even if the authentication challenge succeeds, the presence of `AT_RESULT_IND` in both request and response triggers a **notification message** to explicitly inform the peer (UE) of the result — typically used to convey additional status or policy information.

👉 This use of `EAP-request/AKA'-notification` may carry a success code (e.g., indicating sync success), but it is **required** whenever `AT_RESULT_IND` is echoed back by the UE.

---

### Summary: Conditions Requiring EAP-request/AKA'-notification

| Condition | Trigger |
|--------|--------|
| ✅ Failure in processing EAP-response/AKA'-challenge (e.g., invalid RES, MAC mismatch) | Send **failure-indicating** `EAP-request/AKA'-notification` |
| ✅ `AT_RESULT_IND` was sent in the challenge **and** returned by the UE in the response | Send `EAP-request/AKA'-notification` (can indicate success/failure/synchronization) |

> ⚠️ Note: After sending such a notification, the procedure may continue with either an `EAP-Success` (if ultimately successful) or `EAP-Failure` (if failed), depending on context.

Thus, the **mandatory transmission** of an `EAP-request/AKA'-notification` occurs **on authentication failure** or **when result indication is negotiated via AT_RESULT_IND**.

results.question: What action does the network take regarding timer T3560 when it receives an AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message, and what does it subsequently verify?
results.reference: The network stops timer T3560 and checks the correctness of RES*.
results.model_answer:
According to 3GPP TS 24.501 (as confirmed by the provided context):

- **Action on timer T3560**: Upon receipt of an **AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE** message, the network **stops the timer T3560**.

- **Subsequent verification**: The network **checks the correctness of RES\*** (the authentication response computed by the UE), as defined in TS 33.501.

This is explicitly stated in the first sentence of the context:

> *"Upon receipt of an AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message, the network stops the timer T3560 and checks the correctness of RES* (see 3GPP TS 33.501[24])."*

No other action on T3560 is specified upon receiving AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE — notably, it is *not* restarted or reset; it is unambiguously **stopped**, because its purpose (waiting for the UE’s response to the challenge) is fulfilled.

The verification of RES\* is the core cryptographic check of the 5G AKA procedure: the network compares the UE-provided RES\* against the expected value (XRES\*) derived from the same authentication vector (RAND, SQN, AMF, SQN, and the subscriber’s long-term key K). A match confirms successful mutual authentication.

✅ Therefore, the answer is:

**The network stops timer T3560 and verifies the correctness of RES\*.**

results.question: Under what condition must the network include a different ngKSI value when initiating a new 5G AKA based primary authentication procedure?
results.reference: When the previous 5G AKA procedure completed successfully and the related ngKSI is stored in the network's 5G NAS security context.
results.model_answer:
The network **must** include a different ngKSI value in the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message when initiating a new 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure **if the 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure has been completed successfully and the related ngKSI is stored in the 5G NAS security context of the network**.

This is explicitly mandated by the specification text:

> *"If the 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure has been completed successfully and the related ngKSI is stored in the 5G NAS security context of the network, the network shall include a different ngKSI value in the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message when it initiates a new 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure."*

This requirement ensures that each successful 5G AKA execution results in a *new* ngKSI to uniquely identify the newly established partial native 5G NAS security context (and its associated KAMF). Reusing the same ngKSI would violate the binding between ngKSI and the current KAMF, risking key confusion or replay vulnerabilities.

Additional contextual constraints (which are *also* mandatory but represent *other*, independent conditions) include:
- If an ngKSI is contained in an initial NAS message during a 5GMM procedure, the network **shall select a different ngKSI value** for the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST (appears in both 5G AKA and EAP-based procedure descriptions).
- However, the *primary, definitive condition triggering the "shall" requirement for ngKSI change in the context of *re-initiating 5G AKA* is the prior successful completion and storage of the related ngKSI in the network’s 5G NAS security context.

Note: This requirement does *not* apply to EAP-based procedures in the same way — for EAP, the ngKSI is selected per EAP exchange and tied to the EAP success, but the spec does not state the same “must be different from a previously *stored* one” rule; rather, it mandates difference from any ngKSI present in the *initial NAS message*. The quoted “shall” clause is specific to 5G AKA and explicitly conditioned on successful prior completion and storage.

✅ Therefore, the necessary and sufficient condition is:  
**Successful completion of a prior 5G AKA procedure with the related ngKSI stored in the network’s 5G NAS security context.**

results.question: How does the network react upon receiving an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message with the 5GMM cause '#21 synch failure'?
results.reference: The network stops timer T3560 and may renegotiate with the UDM/AUSF to provide the UE with new authentication parameters.
results.model_answer:
Upon receiving an **AUTHENTICATION FAILURE** message with the **5GMM cause #21 "synch failure"**, the network shall:

- **Stop timer T3560** (as per general rule for AUTHENTICATION FAILURE reception).
- **Use the AUTS parameter** included in the AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message to perform **resynchronization**.

Specifically, according to clause **f)** of the provided context (which corresponds to TS 24.501):

> "Upon the first receipt of an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message from the UE with the 5GMM cause #21 'synch failure', the network shall use the returned AUTS parameter from the authentication failure parameter IE in the AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message, to re-synchronise. The re-synchronisation procedure requires the AMF to delete all unused authentication vectors for that SUPI and obtain new vectors from the UDM/AUSF."

After successful resynchronization:
- The network **shall initiate a new 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure** by sending a new **AUTHENTICATION REQUEST** message with fresh authentication data (including a valid SQN).

Additionally:
- The network may, upon receipt of **two consecutive AUTHENTICATION FAILURE messages with cause #21**, choose to **terminate the authentication procedure** by sending an **AUTHENTICATION REJECT** message (as per NOTE4).

In summary:
✅ On first occurrence:  
→ Use AUTS for resync  
→ Retrieve new authentication vectors from UDM/AUSF  
→ Re-initiate authentication with new challenge  

⚠️ On second consecutive synch failure (optional):  
→ Network may abort and send **AUTHENTICATION REJECT**

results.question: What is the network's immediate procedural step upon receipt of an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message?
results.reference: The network stops the timer T3560.
results.model_answer:
Upon receipt of an **AUTHENTICATION FAILURE** message, the network's immediate procedural step is to **stop timer T3560**.

This action is explicitly specified in the provided context:

> "Upon receipt of an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message, the network stops the timer T3560."

This stoppage of T3560 occurs regardless of the specific 5GMM cause value included in the AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message (e.g., #20 MAC failure, #21 synch failure, #26 non-5G authentication unacceptable, or #71 ngKSI already in use). Stopping T3560 prevents further retransmissions of the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message that triggered the current authentication attempt.

Following this immediate step, the network proceeds based on the **specific 5GMM cause** value and other contextual conditions:

- **Cause #20 (MAC failure)**: The network may initiate an Identification procedure to retrieve SUCI and verify the 5G-GUTI to SUPI mapping. Depending on the outcome, it may send a new AUTHENTICATION REQUEST (if misalignment is found) or AUTHENTICATION REJECT (if correct).
- **Cause #21 (Synch failure)**: The network shall use the AUTS parameter from the AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message to perform resynchronization with the UDM/AUSF, obtain new vectors, and then re-initiate the 5G AKA procedure with a new AUTHENTICATION REQUEST.
- **Cause #71 (ngKSI already in use)**: The network shall select a new ngKSI and re-send the same 5G authentication challenge (AUTHENTICATION REQUEST) with the updated key set identifier.
- **Cause #26 (non-5G authentication unacceptable)**: Similar to #20, the network may initiate identification to verify SUPI/GUTI mapping and respond accordingly with a new AUTHENTICATION REQUEST or AUTHENTICATION REJECT.

Additionally, for any of these causes, if the network receives **three consecutive authentication failures** (with specific conditions on timer T3520 running), the UE may treat the network as untrusted and take local actions (e.g., barring the cell), but this pertains to UE behavior, not the network’s immediate step.

Thus, the **immediate and universal procedural step** taken by the network upon receiving an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message is:
> ✅ **Stop timer T3560.**

results.question: What are the two specific scenarios in which a UE may include the Release assistance indication IE to inform the network?
results.reference: The UE may include it to indicate either that no further uplink or downlink data transmission is expected, or that only a single downlink data transmission (like an acknowledgement) is expected after the uplink, with no further uplink data following that uplink transmission.
results.model_answer:
Based on the provided context from 3GPP TS 24.501, a UE may include the Release assistance indication IE to inform the network in the following two specific scenarios:

1.  **When sending uplink data and expecting no further transmission:** The UE includes the Release assistance indication IE with the DDX field set to "No further uplink and no further downlink data transmission subsequent to the uplink data transmission is expected". This indicates that after sending this uplink data, it does not expect any more uplink or downlink data transmissions.

2.  **When sending uplink data and expecting only one downlink response:** The UE includes the Release assistance indication IE with the DDX field set to "Only a single downlink data transmission and no further uplink data transmission subsequent to the uplink data transmission is expected". This indicates that after sending this uplink data, it expects only one downlink data transmission (e.g., an acknowledgment) but no further uplink data.

These conditions are explicitly defined in clause `h)` of the UL NAS TRANSPORT message handling section:
> h) "CIoT user data container", the AMF shall look up a PDU session routing context for the UE and the PDU session ID, and
> 1) send the content of the Payload container IE towards the SMF identified by the SMF ID of the PDU session routing context; and
> 2) initiate the release of the N1 NAS signalling connection
> i) if the Release assistance indication IE is included in the UL NAS TRANSPORT message and the DDX field of the Release assistance indication IE indicates "No further uplink and no further downlink data transmission subsequent to the uplink data transmission is expected" and if there is no downlink signalling or downlink data for the UE; or
> ii) upon subsequent delivery of the next received downlink data transmission to the UE if the Release assistance indication IE is included in the UL NAS TRANSPORT message and the DDX field of the Release assistance indication IE indicates "Only a single downlink data transmission and no further uplink data transmission subsequent to the uplink data transmission is expected" and if there is no additional downlink signalling or downlink data for the UE

results.question: How does the Release assistance indication IE inform the network about expected data flow when the UE anticipates a response to its uplink transmission?
results.reference: It informs the network that only a single downlink data transmission, such as an acknowledgement or response to the uplink data, is expected, and that no further uplink data transmission will occur after the initial uplink data transmission.
results.model_answer:
The Release assistance indication IE informs the network about expected data flow when the UE anticipates a response to its uplink transmission through the **DDX (Downlink Data Expected) field**.

Specifically, when the UE expects only a single downlink data transmission (such as an acknowledgement or response) following its uplink data transmission and no further uplink data afterwards, it sets the DDX field to:

> **"Only a single downlink data transmission (e.g. acknowledgement or response to uplink data) and no further uplink data transmission subsequent to the uplink data transmission is expected"**

This indicates to the AMF that:
- The UE has completed its uplink data transfer.
- One downlink message (e.g., an ACK or response) is expected from the network.
- After delivering this single downlink transmission, if there is no additional downlink data or signalling pending, the AMF shall initiate the release of the N1 NAS signalling connection.

Thus, this DDX value enables optimized resource management by allowing the network to release the NAS signalling connection after fulfilling the anticipated request-response exchange.

results.question: Why might a UE include the Release assistance indication IE regarding its data transmission expectations?
results.reference: To inform the network about the expected conclusion of data exchange, specifically whether no further data is expected in either direction, or if only a single downlink response is expected after an uplink transmission with no subsequent uplink.
results.model_answer:
A UE includes the **Release assistance indication IE** in a NAS message (e.g., `CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST` or `UL NAS TRANSPORT`) to **signal its data transmission expectations to the network**, enabling the AMF to make **optimized, state-aware decisions about N1 NAS signalling connection release** — specifically, to avoid unnecessary signalling connection maintenance when no further NAS-layer interaction is anticipated.

This is not a request for immediate release, but rather *assistance information* that allows the network to autonomously initiate release *after fulfilling the UE’s stated data exchange intent*, subject to additional conditions (e.g., absence of pending downlink signalling/data).

The specification defines two key DDX (Data Delivery eXpectation) values in this IE that trigger conditional release:

1. **"No further uplink and no further downlink data transmission subsequent to the uplink data transmission is expected"**  
   → The AMF **shall initiate N1 NAS signalling connection release** *if and only if* there is **no pending downlink signalling or downlink data** for the UE at the time of processing (or after delivering any piggybacked uplink data).  
   *(Ref: Context excerpt: “If the DDX field [...] indicates 'No further uplink and no further downlink data transmission [...] the AMF initiates the release...”)*

2. **"Only a single downlink data transmission and no further uplink data transmission subsequent to the uplink data transmission is expected"**  
   → The AMF **shall initiate N1 NAS signalling connection release** *after delivering the next downlink data transmission* **and confirming no additional downlink signalling or data remains pending**.  
   *(Ref: Same context excerpt)*

Thus, the UE includes this IE to:
- **Enable efficient resource usage**: Avoid keeping the NAS signalling connection alive longer than necessary.
- **Support power-efficient operation**: Especially critical for NB-IoT and other CIoT devices where minimizing connection duration reduces energy consumption.
- **Facilitate control-plane optimization**: When combined with CIoT small data containers or CP service requests, it allows the network to complete the entire transaction (e.g., deliver one response) and then cleanly tear down the connection — without requiring an explicit `DE-REGISTRATION REQUEST`.
- **Avoid race conditions or ambiguity**: By declaring its expectation *in advance*, the UE prevents the AMF from erroneously retaining the connection due to uncertainty about whether more data will follow.

Importantly, inclusion of the IE **does not guarantee release**: the AMF *only* acts on the DDX value *if* the corresponding condition on pending downlink traffic is satisfied. If downlink signalling or data *is* pending (e.g., a pending SMF response, SMS, or location reply), the AMF must retain the connection to deliver it — regardless of the DDX value.

In summary: The Release assistance indication IE is a **network-assisted, conditional connection release hint**, allowing the UE to declare its end-to-end data exchange intent so the AMF can perform *timely, deterministic, and optimized* N1 NAS signalling connection release — improving scalability and battery life, especially for massive IoT deployments.

results.question: What does the inclusion of the Release assistance indication IE communicate to the network about future uplink data transmission in the scenario involving a downlink response?
results.reference: It communicates that after the current uplink data transmission, no further uplink data transmission is expected, even though a single downlink transmission (e.g., an acknowledgement) may follow.
results.model_answer:
The inclusion of the **Release assistance indication IE** with its **DDX field** set to a specific value communicates the UE's expectation regarding future uplink and downlink data transmissions after the current uplink transmission.

In the scenario involving a **downlink response**, the relevant setting is:

> **"Only a single downlink data transmission and no further uplink data transmission subsequent to the uplink data transmission is expected"**

This indicates to the network that:
- The UE has sent uplink data.
- The UE expects **one and only one downlink data transmission** (e.g., an acknowledgment or response) from the network as a result.
- After this single downlink transmission, **no further uplink data will be sent by the UE**.

### Network Behavior Implication:
Upon receiving this indication and delivering the next downlink data transmission (the response), if there is **no additional downlink signalling or data pending**, the AMF shall **initiate the release of the N1 NAS signalling connection**.

Thus, the inclusion of the Release assistance indication IE with this DDX value signals that the transaction is effectively complete after the network sends one responsive downlink message, enabling optimized resource management and early release of the signalling connection.

results.question: How does the sender determine the NAS COUNT input for the integrity protection algorithm?
results.reference: The sender uses its locally stored NAS COUNT as the input to the integrity protection algorithm.
results.model_answer:
The sender determines the NAS COUNT input for the integrity protection algorithm by using its **locally stored NAS COUNT**.

### Detailed Explanation:

According to 3GPP TS 24.501, the **sender (either UE or AMF)** maintains a local copy of the NAS COUNT for both uplink and downlink directions, depending on the access type (3GPP or non-3GPP) and whether the context is native or mapped.

- The **NAS COUNT** is a 24-bit value composed of:
  - **8 least significant bits**: NAS sequence number.
  - **16 most significant bits**: NAS overflow counter.

- When used as input to the **integrity protection algorithm**, this 24-bit NAS COUNT is **padded with 8 zero bits in the most significant byte**, forming a **32-bit entity**.

- The sender uses the **current locally stored value** of the appropriate direction's NAS COUNT (uplink for UE sending a message, downlink for AMF sending a message) **before incrementing it** for the next transmission.

- After constructing the SECURITY PROTECTED 5GS NAS MESSAGE:
  - The sender performs integrity protection using this current NAS COUNT.
  - Then, **after transmission**, the sender increments the NAS COUNT by one (handling wraparound from 255 to 0 by incrementing the overflow counter).

> This ensures that each NAS message has a unique sequence number and corresponding NAS COUNT, which is critical for replay protection — except when 5G-IA0 is used, where replay protection is not enforced.

### Key Specification References:
- *"The sender shall use its locally stored NAS COUNT as input to the integrity protection algorithm."*
- *"After each new or retransmitted outbound SECURITY PROTECTED 5GS NAS MESSAGE message, the sender shall increase the NAS COUNT number by one..."*
- NAS COUNT construction: *"concatenated as (NAS overflow counter || NAS sequence number)"*, padded to 32 bits for algorithm input.

Thus, the **input to the integrity protection algorithm is the pre-incremented, locally stored NAS COUNT**, formatted as a 32-bit value.

results.question: What components does the receiver use to form the NAS COUNT for integrity verification, and how are they obtained?
results.reference: The receiver uses the NAS sequence number from the received message and an estimate for the NAS overflow counter (as defined in subclause 4.4.3.1) to form the NAS COUNT input.
results.model_answer:
The receiver forms the **NAS COUNT** for integrity verification using two components: 1. **NAS Sequence Number** – obtained directly from the received NAS message. 2. **Estimated NAS Overflow Counter** – derived based on local logic and state, not transmitted explicitly. --- ### 1. **NAS Sequence Number** - This is the **8 least significant bits (LSB)** of the NAS COUNT. - It is **included in the NAS message header**, specifically as the **Sequence number IE (octet 7)** of the *SECURITY PROTECTED 5GS NAS MESSAGE*. - The receiver extracts this value directly from the received message. --- ### 2. **NAS Overflow Counter (16 most significant bits)** - This is **not transmitted** in the message; instead, the receiver **estimates** it based on its **locally stored NAS COUNT** and replay protection logic. - The estimation follows the rules defined in **subclause 4.4.3.1** (implied by context): > - The sequence number part of the estimated NAS COUNT is taken from the received message. > - The overflow counter is selected such that: > - If the receiver can **guarantee the message is not a replay**, it **may** choose an estimated NAS COUNT **lower than or equal to** the stored NAS COUNT. > - Otherwise, it **must select the overflow counter so that the estimated NAS COUNT is higher than the stored NAS COUNT**. This ensures **replay protection**: each NAS COUNT value is accepted at most once per security context. - The receiver maintains its own **downlink NAS COUNT (for messages from network to UE)** or **uplink NAS COUNT (for messages from UE to AMF)**, depending on direction. - After successful integrity verification, the receiver **updates its stored NAS COUNT** to the **estimated NAS COUNT** used in verification. --- ### Summary: How Receiver Forms NAS COUNT | Component | Source | |--------|--------| | **NAS Sequence Number (8 bits)** | Extracted from the Sequence Number IE in the received NAS message | | **NAS Overflow Counter (16 bits)** | Estimated by receiver using:
– Locally stored NAS COUNT
– Replay detection logic
– Rule: estimated NAS COUNT > stored NAS COUNT unless replay can be ruled out | Then: - The full **24-bit NAS COUNT** = `overflow_counter (16 bits)` || `sequence_number (8 bits)` - When passed to the **integrity algorithm**, it is padded to **32 bits** by adding **8 zero bits at the MSB side**. > ✅ Final input to algorithm: **32-bit value = 0x00 || NAS_OVERFLOW(16) || NAS_SEQUENCE(8)** --- ### Additional Notes - This mechanism enables **robust synchronization** between sender and receiver despite potential message loss or retransmissions. - **Replay protection** is mandatory (except when 5G-IA0 is used), and relies on the correct estimation of NAS COUNT. - The sender always uses its **local stored NAS COUNT** (incremented per transmission), while the receiver must **infer the correct one** for verification.

results.question: What specific octets are included in the integrity protection for a SECURITY PROTECTED 5GS NAS MESSAGE?
results.reference: For a SECURITY PROTECTED 5GS NAS MESSAGE, integrity protection includes octet 7 to n, which encompasses the Sequence number IE and the NAS message IE.
results.model_answer:
According to 3GPP TS 24.501 (and confirmed by the provided context), for a **SECURITY PROTECTED 5GS NAS MESSAGE**, the integrity protection covers:

> **octet 7 to n**, i.e., **the Sequence number IE and the NAS message IE**.

This is explicitly stated in the first paragraph of the context:

> *"a) SECURITY PROTECTED 5GS NAS MESSAGE message, the integrity protection shall include octet 7 to n, i.e. the Sequence number IE and the NAS message IE"*

### Rationale & Structural Confirmation:
- A 5GS NAS message with security header type *SECURITY PROTECTED* (i.e., security header type `101` — see TS 24.501 Table 8.2.1.1) has the following fixed header structure (per clause 8.2.1.1):
  - Octet 1: Extended protocol discriminator  
  - Octet 2: Security header type  
  - Octets 3–6: **Sequence number IE** (4 octets: 1 octet for IEI = `0x77`, 1 octet for length = `0x04`, 2 octets for the 16-bit NAS COUNT value — *but note:* this is the *legacy interpretation*; in reality, per TS 24.501 §8.2.1.1, the Sequence Number IE is encoded as:
    - IEI = `0x77` (1 octet),
    - Length = `0x02` (1 octet),
    - Value = 2-octet NAS COUNT (i.e., lower 16 bits of COUNT) → total **4 octets**.
  - So octets 3–6 = full Sequence Number IE.

- However, the specification **explicitly defines the protected data starting at octet 7**, *not* octet 3. This means:
  - The **integrity algorithm input does NOT include the Sequence Number IE itself**, despite its presence in the message.
  - Instead, the **NAS COUNT value used in the integrity algorithm is derived separately** (from the received Sequence Number IE + overflow estimate — per subclause 4.4.3.1), but the *bytes* of the Sequence Number IE (octets 3–6) are **excluded** from the protected payload.

- Therefore, integrity protection begins **after** the Sequence Number IE — i.e., at **octet 7**, which is the first octet of the **NAS message IE** (e.g., REGISTRATION REQUEST, SECURITY MODE COMMAND, etc.).

- This aligns with the design principle that the *sequence number is used as input to the MAC calculation*, but is *not part of the protected data* — it is transmitted in cleartext (as an IE) to enable receiver-side COUNT reconstruction, while the actual protected content starts with the message body.

### ✅ Final Answer:
**Octets 7 to n**, where:
- Octet 7 is the first octet of the **NAS message IE** (e.g., the Extended Protocol Discriminator of the embedded NAS message), and  
- Octet n is the last octet of that NAS message IE.

The **Sequence Number IE (octets 3–6)** is *not included* in the integrity-protected data — it is used only to derive the NAS COUNT for the MAC computation.

results.question: What action must the receiver take regarding its locally stored NAS COUNT after successfully validating integrity protection?
results.reference: After successful integrity protection validation, the receiver must update its corresponding locally stored NAS COUNT with the value of the estimated NAS COUNT for that NAS message.
results.model_answer:
After successfully validating the integrity protection of a received NAS message, the receiver **shall update its corresponding locally stored NAS COUNT with the value of the estimated NAS COUNT used for the successful integrity verification**.

### Reasoning:
This behavior is explicitly defined in the provided context:

> "After successful integrity protection validation, the receiver shall update its corresponding locally stored NAS COUNT with the value of the estimated NAS COUNT for this NAS message."

This means:
- The receiver forms an **estimated NAS COUNT** using the received NAS sequence number and an inferred NAS overflow counter (based on replay protection logic).
- If the integrity check passes using this estimated NAS COUNT, the receiver updates its own stored downlink (if AMF) or uplink (if UE) NAS COUNT to match this estimated value.
- This ensures synchronization between sender and receiver regarding the sequence state, preventing future integrity failures due to count mismatches.

### Additional Notes:
- For **downlink messages**, the AMF sends with a certain downlink NAS COUNT; upon successful verification, the **UE updates its stored downlink NAS COUNT**.
- For **uplink messages**, after the AMF verifies integrity, it updates its stored **uplink NAS COUNT** for that UE.
- This update only occurs if integrity verification succeeds.
- **Exception**: When 5G-IA0 (null integrity algorithm) is used, integrity verification is not applicable, so no such update based on integrity checking occurs.

Thus, the mandatory action post-successful integrity validation is:  
➡️ **Update the locally stored NAS COUNT to the estimated NAS COUNT used in verification.**

results.question: What are the primary responsibilities of the SMF in relation to PDU connectivity service, and how is the signalling for this service facilitated?
results.reference: The SMF is responsible for session management functions to provide PDU connectivity service to the UE. This service is provided via 5GSM signalling between the UE and SMF, and the session management messages are transferred via the AMF as specified in subclause 8.3.
results.model_answer:
The primary responsibilities of the Session Management Function (SMF) in relation to the PDU connectivity service are defined within the 5G system architecture as per 3GPP TS 24.501 and related specifications.

### **Primary Responsibilities of the SMF:**

The SMF is responsible for session management functions that enable the provision of PDU connectivity services to the User Equipment (UE). These responsibilities include managing the full lifecycle of PDU sessions through standardized procedures, specifically:

1. **PDU Session Establishment (UE-Requested):**  
   The SMF handles the setup of new PDU sessions initiated by the UE, including authentication, authorization, and allocation of network resources.

2. **PDU Session Authentication and Authorization:**  
   The SMF performs or coordinates authentication and authorization procedures between the UE and external data networks (DNs), such as using EAP-based methods or service-level authorization (e.g., for UAS/C2 services).

3. **PDU Session Modification (Both UE-Requested and Network-Requested):**  
   The SMF manages modifications to existing PDU sessions, whether triggered by the UE (e.g., changing QoS parameters) or by the network (e.g., due to policy changes or mobility events).

4. **PDU Session Release (Both UE-Requested and Network-Requested):**  
   The SMF controls the release of PDU sessions, either upon request from the UE or initiated by the network based on inactivity, policy enforcement, or subscription changes.

5. **Handling of Rejection Scenarios:**  
   When a PDU session cannot be established, the SMF creates and sends a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT** message with an appropriate 5GSM cause value (e.g., #27 "missing or unknown DNN", #46 "out of LADN service area", #69 "insufficient resources for specific slice") to inform the UE of the reason.

6. **Policy Enforcement and Subscription Validation:**  
   The SMF validates requests against subscription data and operator policies, including:
   - Checking allowed DNNs, S-NSSAIs, PDU session types, and SSC modes.
   - Enforcing restrictions such as LADN service area boundaries, CAG access, or high-priority access rules.
   - Supporting features like ATSSS (Access Traffic Steering, Switching, and Splitting) for Multi-Access (MA) PDU sessions when enabled.

7. **Support for Emergency and Specialized Services:**  
   The SMF ensures emergency PDU sessions are prioritized and maintained even under access restrictions (e.g., CAG or regional limitations), releasing only non-emergency sessions if needed.

8. **Interaction with Data Networks:**  
   For services requiring interaction with external DN entities (e.g., UAS authorization), the SMF relays authentication/authorization messages (e.g., EAP-failure, service-level-AA response) between the UE and the DN.

---

### **Signalling Facilitation:**

The session management signalling between the UE and the SMF is not direct but is **relayed via the Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF)**. Specifically:

- All 5G Session Management (5GSM) messages are encapsulated within Non-Access Stratum (NAS) messages.
- These NAS messages are transferred between the UE and the AMF over the N1 interface.
- The AMF acts as a transparent relay, forwarding 5GSM messages between the UE and the SMF over the N11 interface.
- This indirect communication ensures separation of concerns: the AMF handles mobility and access-related procedures (5GMM), while the SMF focuses on session control (5GSM).

> As stated in the provided context: *"The session management messages between UE and SMF are transferred via AMF as specified in subclause 8.3."*

Thus, the **signalling path is: UE ↔ AMF ↔ SMF**, with the AMF ensuring proper routing and transport of session management messages without interpreting their content.

---

### Summary

| Responsibility | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| **Session Lifecycle Management** | Establish, modify, and release PDU sessions |
| **Authentication & Authorization** | Coordinate DN-level auth (EAP, service-level AA) |
| **Policy & Subscription Enforcement** | Validate DNN, S-NSSAI, SSC mode, LADN, CAG, etc. |
| **Error Handling** | Send rejection messages with appropriate 5GSM causes |
| **Emergency Services Support** | Prioritize emergency PDU sessions under constraints |
| **Signalling Path** | Messages flow via AMF; no direct UE–SMF NAS link |

This architecture enables scalable, secure, and flexible delivery of PDU connectivity services across diverse use cases in 5G networks.

results.question: How can a UE establish multiple PDU sessions, and what are the possible access network types involved?
results.reference: A UE may establish multiple PDU sessions to the same data network or to different data networks. These sessions can be established via both 3GPP and Non-3GPP access networks simultaneously.
results.model_answer:
A User Equipment (UE) can establish **multiple PDU sessions** simultaneously, either to the **same Data Network (DN)** or to **different DNs**, and these PDU sessions can be established via **3GPP access**, **non-3GPP access**, or **both**. --- ### ✅ How a UE Establishes Multiple PDU Sessions The establishment of multiple PDU sessions is governed by the **5G Session Management (5GSM)** procedures defined in 3GPP TS 24.501. The key procedure for initiating a new PDU session is the: > **UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure** This procedure is: - **Initiated by the UE** - Used to request the creation of a new PDU session - Triggered when the UE needs connectivity to a data network (e.g., for internet access, IMS, LADN, etc.) Each PDU session is identified by a unique **PDU Session ID (PSI)** and is associated with: - A **Single-NSSAI (S-NSSAI)** - A **Data Network Name (DNN)** (if required) - An **access type** (3GPP or non-3GPP) - A **PDU session type** (IPv4, IPv6, IPv4v6, Ethernet, Unstructured) The UE may initiate additional PDU session establishment procedures while other PDU sessions are already active. There is **no inherent limit in the NAS specification** on the number of concurrent PDU sessions a standard UE (WB-N1 mode) can have, although **network and UE capabilities** (e.g., SMF policies, UE storage, radio resources) may impose practical limits. --- ### 📶 Access Network Types Involved Multiple PDU sessions can be established over the following access types: | Access Type | Description | |--------------------|-----------| | **3GPP Access** | Access via cellular networks such as NR (New Radio) or E-UTRA connected to 5GC.
Example: PDU sessions established when the UE is camped on an NR cell. | | **Non-3GPP Access** | Access via untrusted or trusted non-3GPP interworking systems (e.g., Wi-Fi).
The UE connects through the N3IWF (Interworking Function) to the 5GC. | A single UE can have: - Multiple PDU sessions **all over 3GPP access** - Multiple PDU sessions **all over non-3GPP access** - A combination of PDU sessions **over both 3GPP and non-3GPP access simultaneously** > 🔍 From the specification: > _"A UE may establish multiple PDU sessions, to the same data network or to different data networks, via 3GPP and via non-3GPP access networks at the same time."_ Thus, multi-access capability is explicitly supported. --- ### ⚠️ Special Considerations for NB-N1 Mode UEs For **NB-IoT UEs operating in NB-N1 mode**, there are stricter constraints due to reduced capability: - **User-plane resource limitation**: - Maximum of **one** or **two** PDU sessions with active user-plane resources, depending on the "Multiple user-plane resources support bit". - **Control plane optimization preferred**: Small data transfers typically use **control plane CIoT 5GS optimization**, avoiding persistent user-plane setup. - **No simultaneous large numbers of PDU sessions**: Unlike WB-N1 (wideband) UEs, NB-N1 UEs are not expected to handle many concurrent sessions.
